summary: Describes an architecture for indexing distributed databases and applies it to the WHOIS++ directory protocol. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes how to tie many directory servers together so that a search finds the right one. Each server keeps a summary of what the servers below it hold, so a query only travels to the places that could answer it.

questions: how does the whois++ index service work
what is a centroid in a directory index
subtitle: An architecture for indexing many distributed directory servers so a search reaches the right ones.

tldr.problem: A directory built as a rigid hierarchy has to know in advance where an entry sits, so a query whose terms do not fit the name space has to be sent to every server and processed by all of them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts a mesh of index servers above the base servers. Each index server holds a centroid, a list of the templates and the words in the records of the servers below it, and it forwards a query only to the servers that might answer it.
tldr.outcome: Several hierarchies can sit on the same data, special-purpose directories become easy to build, and the same protocols can replicate servers. The RFC is Historic, and its security section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

facts.label: Centroid word delimiter
facts.value: Blank space, newline or the @ character

today: RFC 1913 is a Historic RFC from February 1996. It describes the architecture of the Whois++ Index Service, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its security considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC describes an architecture for indexing in distributed databases and then applies that architecture to the WHOIS++ protocol. The WHOIS++ directory service is intended to be a simple, extensible directory service built on a template-based information model and a flexible query language. The architecture in this document links many WHOIS++ servers together into a distributed, searchable wide area directory service, and it can be used with systems other than WHOIS++ to provide a distributed directory service that is also searchable.

The index service is a set of index servers that sit above the base servers. Each index server holds a summary of what the servers below it contain, and it uses those summaries to decide which servers a query should go to. A base server takes part in the service only if it can produce such a summary for the data it serves.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo describes how to tie many directory servers together so that a search finds the right one. Each server keeps a summary of what the servers below it hold, so a query only travels to the places that could answer it.

sections.title: Why a Hierarchy Was Not Enough
sections.content:
With a vast amount of directory information potentially available on the Internet, it is simply not feasible to build a centralized directory to serve all of it. The usual alternative is a hierarchy of directory information collection agents, where a query is delivered to one agent in the tree and handed up or down until it reaches the agent holding the answer. That approach has been tried before, most notably in some implementations of the X.500 standard, and this RFC sets out to fix its flaws.

The search problem comes first. Recent implementations assume that every entry resides at some location in a hierarchical name space. That is ideal for reading an entry once its location is known, but not for finding the location of entries that meet some set of criteria. When the only criteria known are items which do not appear in the name space, a global query is forced, and a query issued at the root or at the top of a subtree is replicated to all subtrees of the starting point. Every server that receives it must process the query, even if it holds no matching entry, and that part of global query processing is quite expensive. A poorly designed or thin name space sends most queries globally, while a very broad one causes its own navigation problems. Because of these problems, search was turned off at high levels of the X.500 name space.

The location problem follows. With global search off, a user has to know in advance how the name space is laid out to guide a query, and the layout then becomes critical to the user's ability to find the wanted information. There are endless battles over how to lay out the name space and enormous headaches when it turns out to be unsuited to current use, as recently happened in X.500. The Yellow Pages problem is that these implementations are unsuited to easily building and maintaining special-purpose directories, such as one for molecular biologists: the attributes appropriate to the new directory have to be built into the name space, there is a classification problem of how to specify the proper categories, and finding the data to put into the subtree is itself a global search.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory trees work well when you already know where something is, but badly when you are searching for it. A search that cannot be placed in the tree has to go everywhere, and every server then does the work even if it holds nothing that matches.

sections.title: Directory Meshes and Forward Knowledge
sections.content:
Every entry in WHOIS++ has a unique identifier and resides at a specific location in the name space, but the navigational algorithms used to reach an entry no longer depend on the identifier it has been assigned. The index service gets around the name space and hierarchy problems by creating a directory mesh on top of the entries. Each layer of the mesh has a set of forward knowledge that indicates the contents of the various servers at the next lower layer. When a query reaches a server in a given layer, it can prune the search tree and hand the query only to the lower level servers that have indicated they might be able to answer it, so search becomes feasible at all levels of the mesh.

Because the entry identification scheme has been decoupled from the navigation service, multiple hierarchies can be built and easily maintained on top of the existing data, and the user does not need to know in advance where in the mesh an entry is contained. A base level server can be indexed by several index servers, and an index server can index any other server it wishes, so one server can take part in many hierarchies. The Yellow Pages problem becomes tractable as well, because the architecture allows for automatic polling of data and special purpose directories become easy to construct and to maintain.

The protocols that maintain the forward knowledge also work for replication of servers for redundancy and robustness, in which case the forward knowledge handed around is the entire database of entries held by the replicated server. The RFC is careful about the limits of its own idea: the set of information chosen as forward knowledge may or may not be exactly what a truly searchable directory requires, but the protocol itself does not restrict the types of information that can be handed around, and the directory architecture is independent of that choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The mesh is a set of index servers stacked above the data servers. Each index server knows roughly what the servers below it hold, so it can pass a query to only the servers that could answer it.

sections.title: Centroids as Forward Knowledge
sections.content:
The centroid of a server is a list of the templates and attributes used by that server, together with a word list for each attribute. The word list for a given attribute contains one occurrence of every word that appears at least once in that attribute in some record in the server's data, and nothing else. A word is any token delimited by blank spaces, newlines, or the '@' character in the value of an attribute.

The RFC works through an example. A WHOIS++ server holds exactly three records: two User records with the names John Smith and Joe Smith and the favourite drinks Labatt Beer and Molson Beer, and one Domain record with the domain name foo.edu and the contact name Mike Foobar. The centroid for that server lists the template User, with First Name holding Joe and John, Last Name holding Smith, and Favourite Drink holding Beer, Labatt and Molson, and the template Domain, with Domain Name holding foo.edu and Contact Name holding Mike and Foobar.

It is this information that is handed up the tree to provide forward knowledge. The authors suspect there may be a number of different sets of forward knowledge in use in the index service, but the directory architecture is in a very real sense independent of what types of forward knowledge are handed around, and it is entirely possible to build a unified directory that uses many types of forward knowledge at once.
sections.plainLanguage: A centroid is the list of every distinct word in a server's records, grouped by field. An index server can read it and say which server to ask, without asking first.

sections.title: Index Servers, Polling and Referral
sections.content:
An index server collects and collates the centroids, or other forward knowledge, of a number of WHOIS++ servers or of a number of other index servers, and it must itself be able to generate a centroid for the information it holds. When a query arrives in the standard WHOIS++ format, the index server searches its collection of centroids, works out which servers hold records that may fill the query, and then notifies the user's client of the next servers to contact. That referral is the same idea as the referral in the X.500 model, and it is written as a SERVER-TO-ASK block giving the server handle, the host name and the port number, where the port number must be given if it is not the WHOIS++ port 63. An index server may also contain primary data of its own and act as both an index server and a base level server, in which case its answer can be a mix of records and referral pointers.

Centroid propagation is initiated by an authenticated POLL command, which asks for the centroid of any or all templates and attributes held by the polled server. After the polled server has authenticated the poller, it determines which of the requested centroids the poller is allowed to request and then issues a CENTROID-CHANGES report to transmit the data, carrying either the complete centroid or just the changes since the last report, under the ADD, DELETE and FULL operations. When the poller receives the report it can authenticate the pollee before adding the changes to its own data. A polled server that knows which pollers hold its centroid can also signal them by issuing a DATA-CHANGED command, so that the poller can decide if and when to poll again; the RFC includes that command to allow interactive updating of critical information.

The RFC adds reply codes for version 1.0 of the protocol: 113 for a requested compression method that cannot be provided, 227 for an update request that has been acknowledged and logged, 503 for a required attribute missing from an interaction, 504 when the desired server is unreachable, and 505 when the desired server fails to respond to requests but its host is still reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Index servers poll the servers below them for their word lists, and they answer a query by telling the client which servers to ask. When a server's data changes, it can send a message so that the pollers come back for the new list.

sections.title: Hop Counts and Loop Control
sections.content:
There are no prior restrictions on which servers may poll which other servers, and a given server may participate in many sub-meshes, so mechanisms have to be installed to allow cycles in the polling relationships to be detected. The current protocol does this by including a hop count on the polling relationships. Each time a polled server generates forward information, it informs the polling server about its current hop count, which is the maximum of the hop counts of all the servers it polls, plus one. A base level server, one which polls no other servers, has a hop count of zero. When a server decides to poll a new server and its hop count goes up, it must inform all the other servers that poll it about the new hop count. A maximum hop count, 8 in the current version, helps the servers detect polling loops.

A second approach to loop detection puts all the work in the client, which determines which new referrals have already appeared in the referral list and then iterates the referral process until there are no new servers to ask. The RFC points to a separate document for an algorithm that does this in WHOIS++.
sections.plainLanguage: Because any server may poll any other, the protocol counts hops. A server's count is one more than the highest count among the servers it polls, and a base server counts zero. A ceiling of 8 helps the servers notice a loop.

viz.caption: THE PROBLEMS WITH A HIERARCHY, AND WHAT THE MESH CHANGES

cells: A query whose terms do not fit the name space is replicated to every subtree, and every server processes it even when it holds no match
The index server forwards the query only to the servers that said they might match
The user must know the name space layout in advance, and changing it is painful
Entry identification is separate from navigation, so several hierarchies can sit on the same data
The attributes of a special-purpose directory have to be built into the name space, and finding the data for it is itself a global search
Index servers poll automatically, so a special-purpose directory is easy to build and to keep up to date

viz.caption: THE FOUR MESSAGES OF THE INDEX SERVICE

items.title: POLL
items.text: An authenticated request for the centroid of any or all templates and attributes.

items.title: CENTROID-CHANGES
items.text: The answer: the full centroid, or only the changes since the last poll.

items.title: DATA-CHANGED
items.text: A notice that the centroid has changed, so pollers can refresh it.

items.title: SERVER-TO-ASK
items.text: A referral telling the client which server to contact next.
